title: C++ Strings Quick Revision: std::string, string_view and std::format
summary: Night-before revision notes on std::string operations and complexity, SSO, C strings vs std::string, string_view pitfalls, numeric conversions, string streams and std::format.

chapters.title: std::string Mental Model and Core Operations
points: std::string is std::basic_string<char>: owns a contiguous, growable char buffer and tracks size and capacity; guaranteed null-terminated via c_str() and data()
size()/operator[]/front()/back() are O(1); at() is O(1) but bounds-checked and throws std::out_of_range, while operator[] out of range is undefined behaviour
push_back and append(x) are amortised O(1) per char (capacity grows geometrically); insert/erase in the middle are O(n) because the tail shifts
find(x) is O(n*m) worst case and returns std::string::npos (not -1 or 0) when not found; compare the result with npos, never with an int
reserve(n) pre-allocates capacity to avoid repeated reallocation; substr(pos, len) copies O(len) and throws out_of_range if pos > size()

chapters.title: Small String Optimisation and Memory Layout
points: SSO stores short strings inside the string object itself, with no heap allocation (about 15 chars on libstdc++/MSVC, 22 on libc++; implementation-defined)
Past the SSO limit the string allocates on the heap; capacity() of an empty string reveals the inline limit (e.g. 15 on libstdc++)
Moves of SSO strings copy the inline bytes, so std::move on a short string is not a pointer steal; moving a long string steals the heap pointer in O(1)
Because of SSO, pointers, references and iterators into a string are invalidated by moves, swaps and any growth; never keep them across those operations
SSO makes short strings cache-friendly and allocation-free, so prefer by-value std::string for small keys; reserve() only matters once strings exceed the inline buffer

chapters.title: C Strings vs std::string
points: A C string is a char array ending in '\0'; strlen is O(n) because it scans, while std::string::size() is O(1)
Comparing with == on const char* compares addresses, not contents; use strcmp or std::string/string_view == for content
std::string constructs implicitly from const char* (scans for the terminator) and converts back only explicitly via c_str() or data()
std::string can hold embedded '\0' bytes when built with a length (std::string(p, n) or "a\0b"s); C APIs then see only the text before the first '\0'
Comparison row: C string needs manual buffer sizing, strcpy/strcat overflow risk, no ownership; std::string manages memory, grows safely and supports ==, <, + and range-for

chapters.title: std::string_view and Dangling Pitfalls
points: std::string_view (C++17) is a non-owning pointer + length pair; copying is O(1), substr is O(1) with no allocation, and it accepts std::string, const char* and literals
Use string_view for read-only function parameters instead of const std::string&: it avoids a temporary string allocation when passed a literal
Dangling: std::string_view sv = std::string("hi"); or returning a view of a local string leaves sv pointing at freed memory; the view never extends lifetime
Mutating or growing the source string (append, reserve, move) can reallocate and invalidate every view into it

string_view is not guaranteed null-terminated: never pass sv.data() to a C API that expects '\0'; build a std::string first. Also avoid storing views as members or in containers unless the owner clearly outlives them

chapters.title: Conversions and String Streams
points: std::to_string(n) converts int/long/double to string; for double it always uses %f formatting (6 decimals, e.g. 3.140000), so it is poor for floats
stoi/stol/stod throw std::invalid_argument when no digits parse and std::out_of_range when the value overflows; stoi("12abc") returns 12 silently unless you pass a size_t* pos and check it
std::from_chars/to_chars (<charconv>) are the fast, non-throwing, locale-independent option; check the returned ec == std::errc()

std::ostringstream builds a string with << and .str(); std::istringstream parses with >> or std::getline(ss, tok, ',') for splitting; both are slower than to_string/from_chars due to locale and stream overhead
Reuse a stringstream only after ss.str("") and ss.clear(); clear() resets error flags, which a failed extraction leaves set

chapters.title: std::format and Cheat Sheet
points: std::format (C++20, <format>) returns a std::string using {} placeholders: std::format("{} is {}", name, age); format string is checked at compile time, and a mismatched argument count is a compile error
Format specs go after a colon: {:>8} right-align width 8, {:<8} left, {:^8} centre, {:08.3f} zero-padded 3 decimals, {:x} hex, {:#b} binary with prefix, {:+} force sign
Positional args {1} {0} reorder or reuse arguments; literal braces are written {{ and }}; runtime format strings need std::vformat
std::format_to(std::back_inserter(s), ...) appends without a temporary string; std::format_to_n limits output; std::print (C++23) writes directly to stdout

Cheat sheet: size O(1) | find returns npos | stoi throws | to_string(double) gives 6 decimals | string_view never owns | SSO ~15 chars | prefer format over stringstream | Interview Point: why does string_view dangle, what is SSO, to_string vs from_chars, what does find return on failure
